$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b.
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Then, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $R$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by ${R}^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}^{-1}\cdot Rx & ={R}^{-1}\cdot {Q}^{T}b \\ x & ={R}^{-1}\,\,{Q}^{T}\,\,b.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing parts of the equation are ${R}^{-1}$ and $b.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-6d57014e-b23a-5701-a76a-a3703de7149c"] "c8892a71-2970-5d65-891c-76f1124825ea" :question/math-academy-id "q-139796" :question/problem "Given the QR decomposition $A=QR,$ find the least-squares solution to $Ax=b,$ where

$$" :question/worked-solution "The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}3\sqrt{2} & -4\sqrt{2} \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}}x & =\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{2} & 2\sqrt{2} & \sqrt{2} \\ -1 & -1 & 4\end{aligned}]}}\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 9 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}} \\ [\begin{aligned}3\sqrt{2} & -4\sqrt{2} \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}38\sqrt{2} \\ -10\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}3\sqrt{2}{x}_{1}-4\sqrt{2}{x}_{2}=38\sqrt{2} \\ 2{x}_{2}=-10.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}^{-1}\cdot Rx & ={R}^{-1}\cdot {Q}^{T}b \\ x & ={R}^{-1}\,\,{Q}^{T}\,\,b.\end{aligned}

problem for the system

$$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}.$$

We can use QR factorization to construct the least-squares solution of this system. Recall that finding the QR factorization of $A$ means expressing $A$ in the form

$$A = QR,$$

where

- $Q$ has orthonormal columns, and
- $R$ is an upper triangular matrix with positive entries on its main diagonal.

To see how QR factorization can be used to solve a least-squares problem, we first recall that the least-squares solution satisfies the normal equation

$$A^T A \mathbf{x} = A^T \mathbf{b}.$$

Substituting $A = QR,$ we obtain

$$\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, we have $Q^T Q = I.$ Therefore, the above equation becomes

$$R^TR\mathbf{x} = R^TQ^T\mathbf{b}.$$

Since $R^T$ is invertible, pre-multiplying our equation by $(R^T)^{-1}$ gives

$$\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b\end{aligned}$$ which simplifies as

$$R \mathbf{x} = Q^T \mathbf{b}. \qquad\qquad (\ast)$$

The least-squares solution $\hat{\mathbf x}$ can now be found by solving this equation using back-substitution or row operations. This is usually the fastest way.

If we want an explicit formula for the least-squares solution, then we note that since $R$ is invertible, pre-multiplying $(\ast)$ by $R^{-1}$ gives

$$\begin{aligned}{R}^{-1}\cdot Rx & ={R}^{-1}\cdot {Q}^{T}b\end{aligned}$$

which simplifies as

$$\mathbf{x} = R^{-1} Q^T \mathbf{b}.$$

The least-squares solution is unique if $A$ has linearly independent columns." :tutorial/id #uuid "7a9501fc-fdbc-5905-ad31-e3c6c2767a33" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3639 :tutorial/title "Introduction"}
